title: Four points and meeting regions
sections: Planar Radon theorem: Any four labeled points in the plane can be partitioned into two nonempty groups whose convex hulls intersect. Each label is used once. Coincident labels and collinear placements are allowed; intersection at a single point is enough.

The convex hull is the filled stretched-band region: a singleton is a point, two locations give a closed segment, and three noncollinear locations give a filled triangle. The guarantee is sharp: three noncollinear points have no successful split. There are seven unordered splits of four labels: four of type 1+3 and three of type 2+2.

If no three of four distinct points are collinear, exactly one split succeeds: either the crossing diagonals of a convex quadrilateral, or an interior point versus the triangle of the other three. Degenerate placements can have several successful splits. With four labels, the intersection can be a point or segment, but cannot contain a filled triangle.
K–1: Make legal groups and point to an actual shared location. The existing adult launch models a point, a segment and a shaded triangle before the tasks.
Grades 2–3: Organize a complete list, distinguish duplicate splits, and construct arrangements with different successful choices.
Grades 4–5: Separate existence from uniqueness and explain why the guarantee survives collinear and coincident cases; contrast four-point existence with the three-point counterexample.

Trying many placements motivates the four-point conjecture. Checking all seven splits proves a claim about one placement only. A geometric case argument establishes the guarantee for every placement. The detailed tools and complete proof remain on printed pages 4 and 18.
